taxonomy.subtopic: Molecular mimicry and acute inflammatory peripheral demyelination

questions.stem_html:
A 33-year-old man develops tingling in his feet followed by symmetric ascending weakness 10 days after a diarrheal illness. Deep-tendon reflexes are absent. Cerebrospinal fluid has elevated protein with only 2 leukocytes/mm3. Nerve-conduction studies show slowed velocity and conduction block.

Which mechanism most likely initiated this neurologic disorder?

options.text_html: Direct bacterial invasion of anterior horn motor neurons
Deposition of amyloid in dorsal root ganglia after acute infection
Toxin-mediated irreversible blockade of presynaptic acetylcholine release
Autoantibodies against central nervous system myelin basic protein
Antibodies and lymphocytes generated against microbial antigens cross-react with peripheral nerve gangliosides

questions.explanation_html: Microbial epitopes, especially from Campylobacter jejuni, can resemble peripheral nerve gangliosides. The resulting immune response damages myelin or axons, producing rapidly progressive areflexic weakness. The postinfectious timing, albuminocytologic dissociation, and peripheral demyelinating physiology support molecular mimicry against peripheral nerve components.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Campylobacter does not typically invade motor neurons; the neuropathy is immune mediated.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Amyloid neuropathy is chronic and is not linked to an acute postinfectious ascending paralysis.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Botulinum toxin causes descending paralysis with autonomic and cranial findings, not albuminocytologic dissociation.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Guillain-Barre affects peripheral nerves and roots rather than CNS myelin.

questions.educational_objective: Recognize Guillain-Barre syndrome and explain its postinfectious autoimmune pathogenesis through molecular mimicry directed at peripheral nerve gangliosides.
